query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for jet-turbine applications, what single intervention could improve high-temperature mechanical capability while limiting density and preserving room-temperature performance? Formulate one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, its mechanism, the expected improvement relative to a relevant baseline, the temperature and loading conditions under which it should hold, supporting evidence from prior studies, and a decisive experiment with a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a minor vanadium addition (~0.5 mole fraction) into the baseline NbTaHfTiZr refractory high‐entropy alloy will enhance its high-temperature mechanical strength via increased solid solution strengthening and lattice distortion, while its light atomic weight helps limit density and its controlled concentration preserves room-temperature ductility.
generation.material_initial_state: NbTaHfTiZr refractory high‐entropy alloy with a fully disordered BCC solid solution structure displaying good room-temperature ductility.
generation.intervention: Incorporate ~0.5 mole fraction of vanadium into the NbTaHfTiZr alloy to obtain the NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 composition.
generation.conditions: Mechanical performance should be evaluated at high temperatures (≥800 °C) under compressive/tensile loading as well as under room-temperature tensile conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced lattice distortions and solid solution strengthening effects mediated by the vanadium atoms, which integrate into the BCC matrix without triggering deleterious phase separation.
generation.mechanism: Vanadium, when alloyed at a controlled low level, increases lattice distortions that impede dislocation motion at elevated temperatures. This results in higher yield strength at high temperature while its relatively low density and controlled concentration prevent significant increases in overall alloy density and preserve room-temperature plasticity.
generation.predicted_outcome: The NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 alloy is expected to show a high-temperature yield strength improvement of roughly 20–30% compared to the pure NbTaHfTiZr alloy, with room-temperature ductility maintained at levels comparable to the baseline.
generation.baseline: The performance of the standard NbTaHfTiZr refractory HEA without any vanadium addition.
generation.boundary: The effectiveness of this intervention is anticipated primarily in solid solution-based BCC structured refractory HEAs; adding vanadium in excess of the optimized concentration may lead to phase instability or degraded ductility.
generation.uncertainty: While the mechanism of solid solution strengthening is well established, the exact percentage improvement in yield strength and the full temperature dependence remain uncertain until confirmed by experimental testing.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two alloy batches: one of the original NbTaHfTiZr alloy and one of the NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 alloy via similar processing routes. Conduct mechanical tests at high temperatures (≥800 °C) using standardized compression or tensile setups, along with room-temperature tensile tests. Complement the tests with density measurements and microstructural evaluations.
measurements: Phase and microstructure (using XRD and microscopy)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 alloy fails to exhibit at least a 20% increase in high-temperature yield strength over the baseline NbTaHfTiZr alloy or if its room-temperature ductility is significantly compromised (e.g., >10% reduction), then the hypothesis is falsified.

concept of a high configurational entropy favoring the formation of a solid–solution phase, has recently attracted significant attention, and the resulting alloys are known as high-entropy alloys (HEAs) []. As a new class of metallic materials, HEAs or complicated concentrated alloys made up of four or more primary elements greatly increase the alloy design space [,,]. HEA microstructures can be tailored to suit desired qualities, including single-phase solid solution HEAs [,,] and HEAs with hierarchical microstructures [,,,]. Moreover, over a wide temperature range, an increasing number of appealing features in HEAs have been revealed, including an outstanding strength–ductility synergy at ambient temperature [,], extraordinary mechanical capabilities at cryogenic temperatures [], and ultrahigh strength at extreme temperatures [].
